questions.q: Why does Oracle Fusion run some operations as background 'scheduled processes' instead of instantly on screen?
options: Because heavy operations like large reports or bulk imports take real time and shouldn't block the user's screen while they run
Because Oracle wants to slow users down intentionally
Because scheduled processes are only used for security audits
Because instant operations are not allowed in SaaS products
questions.explain: Heavy operations (large reports, bulk imports, allocations) run as background jobs so the user can keep working while the processing happens separately.

questions.q: What can a user do from the Scheduled Processes work area?
options: Only view a list of Oracle employees
Submit, schedule, monitor, and view the output/logs of background jobs
Only change their own password
Only approve purchase orders
questions.explain: The Scheduled Processes work area lets a user submit new jobs, schedule recurring ones, monitor status, and review output or error logs.

questions.q: Which job status means the process is queued but has not yet started?
options: Running
Succeeded
Pending
Warning
questions.explain: Pending means the job is queued and has not yet begun executing; Running means it's actively executing.

questions.q: What does a 'Warning' status on a completed job generally indicate?
options: The job failed completely and produced no output
The job was canceled by the user
The job is still queued
The job completed, but something is worth reviewing
questions.explain: Warning means the job finished but something in the result is worth a second look, distinct from Error (failed) or Succeeded (no issues).

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should be the first troubleshooting step when a user says 'my report never showed up'?
options: Check the Scheduled Processes work area for that job's status and log
Immediately assume the whole application is broken
Restart the user's computer
Submit a new quarterly update request
questions.explain: Checking the job's status and log in Scheduled Processes is almost always the first step — the issue is often a status like Error or Pending, not a broken application.
